In the POSIX sense, a directory is a special file whose content is a sequence of directory entries (struct dirent), each mapping a name to an OS/File/System/Inode number within the same file system.
The directory does not store file content or most metadata — those live in the inode. It is purely a name-to-inode mapping.
Every directory contains two automatic OS/File/System/Link/Hards: . (pointing to itself) and .. (pointing to the parent directory).
In everyday use, "directory" and "folder" are synonyms for a container that organizes files.
In the POSIX data-structure sense, a directory is the mechanism that gives a file its name: the name lives in the directory entry, not in the file itself.
An inode (index node) is the data structure in a Unix-like file system that stores a file's metadata and data-block pointers.
Each inode has a unique number within its file system. The OS/File/System/Directory stores the mapping from names to inode numbers; the inode itself does not store the filename.

A file system link is a name or pointer that lets one file-system location refer to file content or to another path.
The POSIX-core forms are OS/File/System/Link/Hard and OS/File/System/Link/Soft.

Different Types of File System Links
A OS/File/System/Link/Hard is a direct name-to-OS/File/System/Inode mapping: the name is the file object. No path resolution happens; the OS reaches the file directly by inode number.
Different Types of File System Links

A OS/File/System/Link/Soft stores a path string as its payload. Each time it is followed, the OS walks the OS/File/System/Directory tree to resolve that string. If the target has moved or been deleted, the stored string leads nowhere — the link is dangling.

The practical difference: hard links cannot go stale because there is no path to become wrong; symlinks can go stale because the stored path may stop resolving.

File systems separate several ideas that are easy to blur together: bytes on storage, file metadata, directory entries, and pathnames. Links are where those layers become visible.

A hard link is another name for the same underlying file object. On Unix-like file systems, a OS/File/System/Directory maps names to OS/File/System/Inode numbers; multiple hard links are simply multiple directory entries pointing to the same inode, so each name reaches the same file content and metadata.
Deleting one hard link removes that directory entry, not necessarily the file data. The file data remains available until the last hard link is removed and no process still has it open.
Same-object identity - Each hard link is an equal name for the same file, rather than a pointer to a preferred target path.
Rename and deletion resilience - Other hard links keep working when one name is renamed or removed.

No dangling path - A hard link stores no path string — it is a direct name-to-OS/File/System/Inode mapping. There is nothing to go stale: renaming or removing any other hard link to the same inode leaves this one unaffected.
Same-file-system limit - Hard links normally cannot cross file-system boundaries because they refer to an object within one file system.
Directory restrictions - Ordinary users generally cannot hard-link directories, because directory hard links can create cycles and confuse traversal.
Surprising aliasing - Editing through any hard link changes the same underlying file, which can surprise readers who expected a copy.
A symbolic link (also symlink or soft link) is a file whose contents point to another file or directory by storing a path to the target.
Unlike a OS/File/System/Link/Hard, a symbolic link is its own file-system object. When a program follows it, the operating system resolves the stored path and continues at the target.
Cross-boundary references - A symbolic link can point across file systems and, on Unix-like systems, commonly to directories.
Clear indirection - Tools can usually identify the symlink itself and inspect the stored target path.
Flexible organization - Symlinks are useful for config files, tool shims, shared project rules, and compatibility paths where one name should lead somewhere else.
Dangling links - If the target path is moved or deleted, the symlink remains but no longer resolves.
Path sensitivity - Relative symlinks depend on their location; absolute symlinks depend on the same absolute path existing on the current machine.
Traversal complexity - Programs and security checks must decide when to follow symlinks and when to operate on the link itself.

A palimpsest is a writing surface reused after an earlier text has been erased or scraped away, while traces of the earlier writing remain. By extension, it describes something whose present form carries marks of earlier forms beneath it.
The image fits a knowledge garden when a page brings an original source together with later commentary: the source remains legible, while annotations add another layer of meaning.

Medieval scribes reused parchment because preparing it was costly. Erasing the surface did not always remove the earlier text completely, leaving the older writing partly legible beneath the new text.
A literal manuscript palimpsest reuses one physical surface. A digital garden can preserve distinct source and commentary pages, then present them together as a layered reading.
A source page can remain the record of what another garden says, while a local discussion page holds interpretation and response.

A Database/View can present the source and commentary together without making either layer stand in for the other. The combined view is palimpsestic in its reading experience, though the underlying digital pages are separate.
Palimpsest · French Ministry of Culture defines the manuscript form as reused parchment where the erased original remains partly readable.

A paradox is a statement or situation that seems self-contradictory or absurd yet is supported by reasoning that looks sound. From the Greek paradoxon, "contrary to expectation."

Veridical — the conclusion sounds absurd but is true. The Monty Hall problem and the birthday paradox, in which 23 people are enough for even odds that two share a birthday, both hold up under calculation.
Falsidical — the conclusion is false because the argument hides a mistake. Zeno's paradoxes of motion fall apart once an infinite sum of shrinking steps is allowed to add up to a finite distance.

Antinomy — accepted reasoning leads to a true contradiction, which forces a change to the assumptions. The liar paradox ("this sentence is false") and Russell's paradox about the set of all sets that do not contain themselves are the classic cases; Russell's led to the axioms of modern set theory.

A paradox marks the spot where an intuition or a theory breaks. Working one out usually means giving up an assumption nobody had noticed they were making, which is why paradoxes have driven changes in logic, mathematics and physics.
Person/Erwin Schrödinger/Cat is a paradox built on purpose, to show where a theory of quantum measurement leads.

Parallax is the apparent shift in an object's position when it is seen from two different places. Near objects shift more than far ones, so the size of the shift tells how far away something is.
By extension, viewing one subject from several positions reveals a dimension that no single view shows.
Hold a finger at arm's length and close each eye in turn: the finger jumps against the background. Move the finger closer and the jump grows.
The brain merges the two slightly different views from the two eyes into a sense of depth, a process called stereopsis.

Astronomy. As the Earth travels around the Sun, a nearby star shifts against more distant stars. Measuring that shift from opposite sides of the orbit gives the star's distance. A parsec is the distance at which the shift is one arcsecond.

Web design. Parallax scrolling scrolls background layers more slowly than foreground layers, so a flat page appears to have depth. Website/Misato Town gets a related effect another way, by tying scroll position to an animation timeline.

Layered media. A recording published in several layers, from raw session to finished piece, lets a listener compare versions of the same moment, as with the layers planned for GitP/A in Week/Review/26/10/11 Sun. A Palimpsest and a show their subject in layers in a similar way.
